title: Class 5 Maths Be My Multiple, I'll Be Your Factor (Chapter 6 Guide) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Be My Multiple Ill Be Your Factor Guide
meta_desc: A clear Class 5 Maths Be My Multiple Ill Be Your Factor guide: factors, multiples, common ones, chapter games and a free 8-question quiz. Start now.
excerpt: NCERT Chapter 6 turns factors and multiples into a game of catch. Here is how the ideas fit together, with a worked case study and a quick quiz your child can try.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
The title alone confuses parents the first time they see it. Class 5 Maths Be My Multiple, I’ll Be Your Factor sounds like a riddle, and that is the whole point — NCERT Chapter 6 teaches factors and multiples as a two-way relationship between numbers, not two lists to memorise. When a child says ‘6 is a factor of 24’, the very same fact means ‘24 is a multiple of 6’. One sentence, two names, depending on which number you stand on. Get that idea and the rest of the chapter falls into place.

I have taught this chapter to Class 5 groups in a Tier-2 town where most kids arrived thinking ‘factor’ and ‘multiple’ were interchangeable. They are opposites, in a sense, and the chapter’s games are built to make that click. Let me walk through what actually matters.

What a factor is, in plain words

A factor of a number divides it exactly, leaving no remainder. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 — each one splits 12 into equal groups with nothing left over. Ask a child to arrange 12 counters into equal rows and they will discover the factors by hand: 1 row of 12, 2 rows of 6, 3 rows of 4. Every neat rectangle is a factor pair. This is the ‘I’ll be your factor’ half of the title.

One honest caveat I always flag: 1 is a factor of every number, and every number is a factor of itself. Children forget these two and lose easy marks. Drill them.

What a multiple is

A multiple is what you get in the times table. The multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and so on — the list never ends. So 24 is a multiple of 6 because 6 × 4 lands exactly on 24. This is the ‘be my multiple’ half. Notice the direction: a number has a finite set of factors but an endless run of multiples.

The relationship the chapter is really about

Here is the counter-intuitive bit most kids miss. Factor and multiple are the same link seen from two ends. If 4 is a factor of 20, then 20 is automatically a multiple of 4. You never have to check both — proving one proves the other. NCERT drives this home with a partner game: one child names a number, the other must say a valid multiple or factor of it and explain which. That back-and-forth is the lesson.

Common factors and common multiples

Once single numbers are comfortable, the chapter pairs them up. A common factor divides two numbers exactly. A common multiple appears in both times tables. Take 8 and 12: their common factors are 1, 2 and 4; their smallest common multiple is 24. The table below lays it out.

IdeaQuestion to askExample (8 and 12)
Factors of eachWhat divides it exactly?8: 1,2,4,8   12: 1,2,3,4,6,12
Common factorsWhich appear in both lists?1, 2, 4
Multiples of eachWhat is in its times table?8,16,24,32   12,24,36
Common multiplesWhich appear in both?24, 48, 72…

Notice the chapter stops short of the formal terms HCF and LCM. That comes later. Here the language stays concrete — ‘common factor’, ‘smallest common multiple’ — because the goal is understanding, not vocabulary.

The chapter games that make it stick

NCERT wraps the ideas in puzzles, and they genuinely work better than plain sums. A few I lean on:

  • Grouping counters — give 18 beads and ask for every way to make equal groups. Each way is a factor pair.
  • The hopping game — a frog jumps in steps of 3 on a number line; where it lands are the multiples of 3.
  • Even, odd and primes — a number with exactly two factors (1 and itself) is prime. The chapter has children hunt for numbers with only two factors.
  • Find the mystery number — clues like ‘a multiple of 5, a factor of 30, less than 20’ that narrow to one answer (15).

A worked case study

This is the kind of passage the chapter and the companion e-book use. Read it, then solve.

Meera is packing sweets for Diwali. She has 24 laddoos and 36 barfis. She wants to make identical gift boxes so that every box has the same number of laddoos and the same number of barfis, with none left over.

Question 1: What is the largest number of boxes she can make? The number of boxes must be a common factor of 24 and 36. Factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24; factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. The common factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 — and the largest is 12. So Meera can make 12 boxes.

Question 2: How many of each sweet go in a box? Split 24 laddoos into 12 boxes: 2 each. Split 36 barfis into 12 boxes: 3 each. Every box gets 2 laddoos and 3 barfis, nothing wasted. The idea of a common factor did the whole job — no guessing.

quiz.title: Class 5 Factors and Multiples Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions from NCERT Chapter 6, Be My Multiple, I'll Be Your Factor. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 5 factors, multiples and common ones

questions.q: Which of these is a factor of 18?
questions.explanation: 6 divides 18 exactly (18 divided by 6 is 3, no remainder). 4, 8 and 5 do not.

questions.q: What are the first four multiples of 7?
questions.explanation: Multiples come from the times table: 7 times 1, 2, 3, 4 gives 7, 14, 21, 28.

questions.q: If 9 is a factor of 45, which statement is also true?
questions.explanation: Factor and multiple are the same link seen two ways. If 9 is a factor of 45, then 45 is a multiple of 9.

questions.q: How many factors does a prime number have?
questions.explanation: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and the number itself. For example, 7 has only 1 and 7.

questions.q: Which number is a common factor of 12 and 20?
questions.explanation: 4 divides both 12 and 20 exactly. 5 divides only 20, 6 only 12, and 8 divides neither.

questions.q: What is the smallest common multiple of 4 and 6?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12... Multiples of 6: 6, 12... The first shared one is 12.

questions.q: Which number is a factor of every whole number?
questions.explanation: 1 divides every number exactly, so 1 is a factor of every whole number.

questions.q: I am a multiple of 5, a factor of 30, and less than 20. Which number am I?
questions.explanation: 15 is a multiple of 5, divides 30 exactly, and is under 20. It fits all three clues.

faq.q: What is Chapter 6 of Class 5 Maths about?
faq.a: It teaches factors and multiples and how they are linked. If one number is a factor of another, the second is a multiple of the first. It also covers common factors, common multiples and prime numbers, all through games and puzzles rather than dry rules.

faq.q: What is the difference between a factor and a multiple?
faq.a: A factor divides a number exactly — the factors of 10 are 1, 2, 5 and 10. A multiple is what you reach in the times table — the multiples of 10 are 10, 20, 30 and so on. A number has only a few factors but endless multiples.

faq.q: How do you find common factors of two numbers?
faq.a: List the factors of each number, then pick the ones that appear in both lists. For 12 and 18 the factors shared are 1, 2, 3 and 6, so those are the common factors.

faq.q: Does this chapter teach HCF and LCM?
faq.a: Not by those names. Class 5 stays with the plain ideas of common factors and the smallest common multiple. The formal HCF and LCM methods come in a later class, so keep the language concrete here.

faq.q: Where can I get case studies with solutions for this chapter?
faq.a: Our Class 5 Be My Multiple, I'll Be Your Factor case-study e-book has real-life passages like the Diwali gift-box problem, each with fully worked solutions and practice MCQs — an instant PDF you can print. The link is in the box below.
